design_detail: Controlled oral administration study on a closed research ward. Eight volunteers received four daily 10-mg doses of S-(+)-methamphetamine hydrochloride as a sustained-release tablet formulation within 7 days; three weeks later five of them received four daily 20-mg doses. Doses were given under subject-blind conditions with placebo capsules at other times, in a fixed order (low regimen first). Plasma was sampled to 24 h and oral fluid to 72 h in the first session of each regimen, with 200 plasma and 590 oral fluid specimens analysed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry; three oral-fluid collection methods were compared, and heart rate, blood pressure, respiration, oxygen saturation, temperatures and pupil diameter were recorded in the first session of each regimen and in a placebo session.
can_establish: Plasma and oral-fluid concentration–time profiles, half-life, time to peak and detection windows for methamphetamine and its metabolite amphetamine after a sustained-release oral formulation, in 8 volunteers; how much oral-fluid concentrations depend on the collection method; and whether oral-fluid concentrations can predict plasma concentrations.
cannot_establish: The pharmacokinetics of methamphetamine as people usually take it (the formulation was a sustained-release pharmaceutical given by mouth, and time to peak is formulation-dependent); dose-proportionality beyond two dose levels given in a fixed order to partly different people; and the physiological effects of these doses with any precision, since those analyses rest on five participants.

sample.recruitment: Volunteers resident on the secure clinical ward of the National Institute on Drug Abuse Intramural Research Program, Baltimore; the recruitment route is not described (p. 122).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Medical, physical and psychological evaluation before admission, including a history of past and recent drug use; participants lived on the closed ward for two weeks before the first dose so that previously self-administered drugs would be eliminated (p. 122). No other eligibility criteria are given.
sample.demographics: Four men and four women; mean age 35.3 years (SD 4.2, range 26.3–39.8); mean height 171.5 cm (SD 9.8, range 149.9–177.8); mean weight 72.0 kg (SD 17.6, range 54.7–103.2) (p. 124). Their own pattern of methamphetamine use is not reported.
sample.attrition: Two participants were disqualified for medical reasons and a third chose to stop after the fourth dose, so only five of the eight received the 20-mg regimen; no plasma was obtained from one participant after the first 10-mg dose because of blood-collection difficulties, and no physiological data were collected for one participant (pp. 122–124).
sample.selection_effects: A small residential sample with no reported characterization of the participants' own drug use, studied under two weeks of supervised abstinence; whoever remained for the second regimen had tolerated the first, so the 20-mg results come from a selected five.

exposure.measurement: Drug administered on the ward and measured directly: methamphetamine and amphetamine in plasma and oral fluid by solid-phase extraction and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry, with limits of detection and quantification of 2.5 µg/L for both analytes and between-run imprecision of 1.4–12% across control concentrations (pp. 123–124).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: four daily oral doses of 10 mg, and in five participants four daily oral doses of 20 mg three weeks later, each as one or two 10-mg sustained-release tablets inside a gelatin capsule with lactose filler; placebo capsules contained lactose alone. The formulation releases 20–40% of the drug within 30 minutes, 35–55% within 1 hour and 60–80% within 4 hours. The authors state they chose a sustained-release oral formulation for participant safety, although methamphetamine is less commonly taken by mouth (p. 122).
exposure.polysubstance: Two weeks of residence on a closed ward before dosing is the control for other drug use; no urine screening results, tobacco use or caffeine use are reported (p. 122).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Two weeks on a closed ward before the first dose; three weeks between the two regimens (p. 122).

comparison.controls: Placebo sessions within the same participants provide the comparison for the physiological measures; there is no separate control group and no placebo comparison for the pharmacokinetics.
comparison.matching: Within-person, but the two dose levels were given in a fixed order (10 mg first, 20 mg three weeks later) and to partly different people, so dose is confounded with time and with who remained in the study.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the pharmacokinetics. For the physiological comparisons, tolerance acquired during the first regimen cannot be separated from the dose difference, because the high dose always came second.

outcomes.instruments: Non-compartmental pharmacokinetics (WinNonlin): lag time, time to peak, peak concentration, half-life by log-linear regression of the terminal phase, AUC from dosing to 24 h by the trapezoidal rule, volume of distribution and total body clearance; a one-compartment model with first-order input and output for the plasma profiles. Three oral-fluid collection methods (citric-acid candy-stimulated expectoration, citric-acid-treated cotton swab, neutral cotton swab) and pH indicator sticks with a resolution of 0.4 pH units. Physiological measures with a bedside monitor and pupillometry with an adapted camera (pp. 122–124).
outcomes.validity_norms: Assay validated in-house with stated imprecision; oral-fluid pH measured only to within 0.4 units, which the authors do not discuss as a limitation when interpreting the pH-dependence of concentrations.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Detection window' is the time over which concentrations stay at or above 2.5 µg/L, or above the cutoffs proposed in 2001 by the US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (50 µg/L methamphetamine with amphetamine at or above the limit of quantification); 'detection rate' is the proportion of specimens positive in a time period.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported beyond post-hoc Scheffé and Bonferroni tests inside each ANOVA; the α level was 0.05 throughout (p. 124). Fourteen pharmacokinetic parameters are tabulated per dose level, and about six inferential analyses are reported (AUC by dose; oral-fluid AUC by dose, device and subject; pH by device and subject; the oral fluid–plasma regression; physiological AUCs by dose).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Administration was subject-blind only; no blinding of staff is described. Assays are objective and were run against calibrators and controls.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means (SD) with ranges; no confidence intervals except for the ratios between collection devices. Plasma after the first dose, 10 mg (n=7 with plasma) and 20 mg (n=5): lag time 1.5 (SD 0.8) and 1.1 (SD 0.5) h; time to peak 5.4 (SD 2.5) and 7.5 (SD 3.4) h; peak 20.2 (SD 6.4) and 32.4 (SD 7.7) µg/L; half-life 9.3 (SD 3.7) and 11.1 (SD 7.2) h; AUC to 24 h 269.1 (SD 94.3) and 468.1 (SD 151.8) h·µg/L; volume of distribution 5.8 (SD 2.6) and 5.3 (SD 2.1) L/kg; clearance 32.2 (SD 13.7) and 33.5 (SD 15.9) L/h. Oral fluid: time to peak 5.0 (SD 1.9) and 4.7 (SD 3.9) h; peak 106.1 (SD 100.8) and 192.2 (SD 120.8) µg/L; half-life 7.1 (SD 2.3) and 8.1 (SD 1.9) h (Table 1, p. 125). Plasma AUC was 2.1 (SD 0.7) times higher after the high dose (P = 0.009). Amphetamine AUC was 21% (SD 25%) of methamphetamine in plasma and 24.0% (SD 11.4%) in oral fluid on a molar basis. Oral-fluid AUCs were 3.8 (SD 2.3) times the plasma AUCs (P = 0.009); the oral fluid-to-plasma ratio had a median of 2.0 and ranged from 0.0 to 23.0 (n=67), and the regression of oral-fluid on plasma concentrations gave R² = 0.222 (P = 0.005) (pp. 125–127).
analysis.covariates: Mixed-effects models with subject as a random effect for the oral-fluid analyses; no adjustment for sex, weight or oral-fluid pH in the pharmacokinetic comparisons.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the study was approved by the institutional review board.
analysis.selective_reporting: Pharmacokinetic results for the other two oral-fluid collection methods are placed in an online data supplement that was not read for this card; urine results are cited to a separate publication by the same group.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. Eight participants (five at the higher dose) with standard deviations approaching or exceeding the means for several oral-fluid parameters (peak 106.1 ± 100.8 µg/L; AUC 1118.0 ± 983.4 h·µg/L) make every oral-fluid estimate imprecise.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After a sustained-release oral formulation, plasma methamphetamine appeared within 0.25–2 h, peaked at about 5–8 h and had a half-life of about 9–11 hours; amphetamine reached about a fifth to a quarter of the parent drug's AUC and peaked later. Oral-fluid concentrations were on average about twice to four times plasma concentrations but varied so widely, and depended so much on the collection method and on oral-fluid pH, that they could not predict plasma concentrations (R² 0.222).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion that oral fluid is practical for detecting use but inferior to urine in concentration and detection window follows from the data. Two cautions for anyone citing the pharmacokinetics: the time to peak (5.4–7.5 h) belongs to this sustained-release formulation, as the authors show by comparing it with 2.9–3.6 h for other oral formulations, while the half-life is formulation-independent and agrees with other studies; and the cardiovascular findings rest on five participants and only two of eight physiological measures reached significance, so they bound the effects of these doses rather than establishing them. The paper repeatedly describes 13 person-sessions as '13 individuals' although only 8 people took part.

timeline.event: Oral methamphetamine pharmacokinetics with repeated daily dosing (Cook et al., 1992): half-life 9.1–11.2 h, time to peak 2.9–3.3 h with a capsule formulation
Smoked and intravenous pharmacokinetics in 6 men: half-life 11.1–12.2 h
Intranasal and smoked bioavailability and pharmacokinetics in 8 men: half-life about 10.7 h by both routes
Intravenous enantiomer study: d-methamphetamine half-life 10.2–10.7 h, l-methamphetamine 13.3–15.0 h, showing that the half-life quoted for 'methamphetamine' depends on which isomer was given

replication.where_it_stands: The half-life of about 10 hours is now consistent across oral, smoked, intranasal and intravenous studies from three laboratories. Time to peak is formulation- and route-dependent and should never be quoted without both. The oral fluid-to-plasma relationship remains too variable for oral fluid to stand in for plasma concentrations, which later oral-fluid work has not overturned.

funding.funder: Intramural Research Program of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health: the acknowledgements state that the research was sponsored by NIDA Intramural Research Program funds (p. 132); the authors' affiliations are on p. 121.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: One author is affiliated with Amgen Inc. (Clinical Affairs) and one with a private research company, ConeChem Research; the study drug was a commercial sustained-release product. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results (p. 121).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized crossover of an immediate-release and a sustained-release oral dose with the same participants, balanced in order, with plasma sampling beyond 24 hours so that the terminal phase is captured, oral-fluid pH measured with a meter rather than indicator sticks, and enough participants to estimate the oral fluid-to-plasma ratio with a usable interval.

domains.note: No randomization: every participant received the 10-mg regimen first and, if still in the study, the 20-mg regimen three weeks later, so dose is confounded with order, with time on the ward and with who remained. RoB 2 is used because the design enum has no category for a fixed-order controlled administration study; the editors note that no validated instrument fits this design.
Administration was subject-blind with placebo capsules, but staff blinding is not described and the dose sequence was known; dosing itself was supervised on a closed ward, so adherence is secure.

Three of eight did not complete the second regimen (two disqualified medically, one withdrew), one participant has no plasma data for the first dose and one no physiological data; the physiological analyses rest on five participants.
Validated gas chromatography–mass spectrometry with calibrators and duplicate controls in each batch; automated physiological monitoring.

No protocol; two of the three collection methods are reported only in an online supplement; the modelling parameters appear with different values and units in the Results and the Discussion (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The assays and the controlled residential setting are strengths, and the concentration–time data are the most reliable part of the paper. The overall judgment is set by the fixed dose order with substantial attrition before the higher dose, which makes the dose comparison and the physiological results weak. The source can be cited for the plasma and oral-fluid pharmacokinetics of a sustained-release oral formulation (half-life, time to peak, peak concentration, amphetamine ratio), for the dependence of oral-fluid concentrations on the collection method and pH, and for detection windows; it cannot be cited for dose-proportionality, for time to peak after other oral preparations, or for precise cardiovascular effects.

key_findings.finding: After the first 10-mg sustained-release oral dose, plasma methamphetamine peaked at 20.2 µg/L (SD 6.4) at 5.4 h (SD 2.5), with a lag of 1.5 h (SD 0.8) and a half-life of 9.3 h (SD 3.7); after the first 20-mg dose, peak 32.4 µg/L (SD 7.7) at 7.5 h (SD 3.4) with a half-life of 11.1 h (SD 7.2).

The overall mean plasma half-life was 10.0 h (SD 5.2) and did not differ between doses; the authors place it alongside previously reported values of 9.1–13.1 h after oral, inhaled and intravenous dosing.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'In our study, plasma METH half-lives were not dose dependent' (p. 128); Table 3 (p. 130)
key_findings.note: The comparison values in Table 3 are taken from other published studies, not measured here.

key_findings.finding: Time to peak with this sustained-release formulation (overall mean 6.3 h, SD 3.0) was longer than the 2.9–3.6 h reported for other oral formulations, including a study using the same product with more frequent sampling (3.0 h).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Mean plasma METH tmax values reported in our study' (p. 128)

key_findings.finding: Plasma AUC over 24 h was 2.1 times higher (SD 0.7, range 1.2–3.1) after the 20-mg than after the 10-mg dose (P = 0.009).
key_findings.locator: Results › METH and AMP pharmacokinetics in plasma and oral fluid, 1st paragraph after Table 1

key_findings.finding: Amphetamine, the active metabolite, peaked later than the parent drug (plasma time to peak 11.9 h, SD 6.9, after the low dose and 14.3 h, SD 5.5, after the high dose) and reached a 24-h AUC of 21% (SD 25%) of methamphetamine in plasma and 24.0% (SD 11.4%) in oral fluid, on a molar basis.
key_findings.locator: Results › METH and AMP pharmacokinetics in plasma and oral fluid, 2nd paragraph (p. 125) and the oral-fluid paragraphs (p. 125); Table 2 (p. 127)

key_findings.finding: Oral-fluid concentrations were higher than plasma concentrations (mean AUC ratio 3.8, SD 2.3, range 1.8–8.7; P = 0.009), but the oral fluid-to-plasma ratio was highly variable within and between people (median 2.0, range 0.0–23.0, n=67) and plasma concentrations could not be predicted from oral fluid (R² = 0.222, P = 0.005).
key_findings.locator: Results › METH and AMP pharmacokinetics in plasma and oral fluid, last three paragraphs (p. 125; the last continues at the top of p. 127); Figure 2 (p. 127)

key_findings.finding: The collection method changed the measured concentration: AUCs from neutral cotton swabs were on average 1.47 times those from citric-acid-treated swabs and 1.92 times (95% CI 1.06–3.51; P<0.05) those from citric-acid candy-stimulated expectoration, with significant effects of dose (P<0.001), device (P = 0.006) and subject (P = 0.003).
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of the different oral fluid collection methods, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Oral-fluid pH differed sharply by device: 2.8 (SD 0.3) with citric-acid-treated swabs, 4.3 (SD 0.8) with candy stimulation and 6.0 (SD 0.6) with neutral swabs (both device and subject P<0.001), which is the mechanism the authors propose for the concentration differences.

Detection at 24 hours after a single dose: plasma methamphetamine exceeded 2.5 µg/L in 5 of 7 participants after 10 mg (4.8–6.9 µg/L) and 4 of 5 after 20 mg (5.2–15.9 µg/L), while all candy-stimulated oral-fluid specimens at 24 h were positive (2.5–33.2 and 10.5–68.1 µg/L).
key_findings.locator: Results › Windows of detection, 1st paragraph (plasma) and 2nd paragraph (oral fluid)

key_findings.finding: After four doses, methamphetamine remained above 2.5 µg/L in candy-stimulated oral fluid for 36–72 h (mean 58.3 h, SD 14.5); 48 h after the last dose all specimens were below the cutoffs proposed by the US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (50 µg/L methamphetamine with amphetamine at or above the limit of quantification).
key_findings.locator: Results › Pharmacologic effects, preceding paragraph on SAMHSA cutoffs (p. 128); Discussion, paragraph beginning 'After four 10- or 20-mg doses' (p. 131)
key_findings.note: The Results (p. 127) print the same window as 36–76 h; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: With those proposed cutoffs applied to this study, only 1 of 13 person-sessions was positive 24 h after a single dose, and 23 of 130 specimens collected within 24 h of dosing met them (18%).
key_findings.locator: Results › SAMHSA cutoff paragraph (p. 128); Discussion, windows-of-detection paragraph (p. 131)

key_findings.finding: Physiological effects of these oral doses were modest: across 12-hour AUCs, only diastolic blood pressure (+10.1%, P = 0.003) and heart rate (+21.7%, P = 0.036) differed from placebo, and only at 20 mg; systolic blood pressure, skin and core temperature, oxygen saturation and pupil diameter did not differ. The analysis rests on five participants.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1, the Range column of the 20-mg oral-fluid block is displaced by one row: the half-life row has no range, the AUC row carries '5.5–10.5' (which fits the half-life), the volume-of-distribution row carries '673.8–3891.0' (which fits the AUC), and the clearance row carries '4.5–24.7'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Three of the four printed ranges in that block belong to the row above; anyone reading ranges from this table for the 20-mg oral-fluid parameters will take the wrong values.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's column heading says '10 mg (n = 8)' for both the plasma and the oral-fluid blocks, although footnote b states that no plasma samples were collected from one volunteer and the Results give n = 7 for the plasma peak.
reporting_issues.consequence: The plasma parameters at the low dose rest on 7 participants, not 8.

reporting_issues.issue: The one-compartment model parameters are given twice with different values and different units: the Results print K01 as 1.07 ± 0.60 h and K10 as 10.76 ± 4.20 h (n = 13), while the Discussion gives K01 = 0.93 ± 0.61 h⁻¹ and K10 = 0.085 ± 0.067 h⁻¹ for the same fits. Rate constants cannot have units of hours, and a K10 of 10.76 h⁻¹ would imply an elimination half-life of about 4 minutes, against the measured 9–11 hours.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Results values are unusable; the Discussion values are the internally consistent ones (0.693/0.085 = 8.2 h, editors' calculation) and are the ones that can be compared with the other studies cited there.

reporting_issues.issue: The model fits are reported for n = 13 although only 12 plasma profiles exist (7 at the low dose plus 5 at the high dose), as the paper itself implies when it reports initial plasma detection for n = 12.
reporting_issues.consequence: One profile in the modelling count is unaccounted for; the discrepancy is small but it is the same count (13) that is elsewhere described as '13 individuals'.

reporting_issues.issue: Person-sessions are repeatedly called individuals: '8 of 13 individuals', '1 of 13 individuals', '9 of 12 participants', although only 8 people took part, 5 of them twice.
reporting_issues.consequence: Detection rates read as if they came from 12 or 13 people; they come from 8, which makes them less independent and the proportions less precise than they appear.

reporting_issues.issue: In the discussion of oral-fluid detection, work by Suzuki et al. is cited as reference 17, which in this article's list is Cook et al. (1993) on smoked methamphetamine; Suzuki et al. is reference 22.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader following the citation lands on the wrong paper; the 48-hour oral-fluid detection in two cases belongs to Suzuki et al.

reporting_issues.issue: The detection window after four doses is printed as 36–76 h in the Results (p. 127) but as 36–72 h (mean 58.3, SD 14.5) in the abstract (p. 121) and the Discussion (p. 131).
reporting_issues.consequence: The upper end of the window differs by 4 hours between sections and the paper does not say which is right; key finding 9 uses the Discussion's 36–72 h.
